title: Ogilvy's observatory at Ottershaw
place: A small, dark Victorian observatory on high ground above Ottershaw and Chertsey. A brass telescope driven by ticking clockwork points up through a narrow oblong slit in the domed roof, and a band of stars shows through the gap. A shuttered lantern in one corner throws a faint pool of light on the wooden floor. A little table nearby holds a soda siphon. Everything else is soft blackness, with the warm night air coming in through the slit.
why: It is the book's first quiet, intimate space: a dark, ticking room open to the stars, perfect for long, calm reading.
excerpts: the black and silent observatory, the shadowed lantern throwing a feeble glow upon the floor in the corner
the steady ticking of the clockwork of the telescope, the little slit in the roof—an oblong profundity with the stardust streaked across it
Looking through the telescope, one saw a circle of deep blue and the little round planet swimming in the field.
to the little table where the siphon stood

title: The sand pits on Horsell Common at dawn
place: An open heath of heather and sandy turf near the sand pits between Horsell, Ottershaw and Woking. A great fresh crater has been torn into the ground, ringed by heaps of flung sand and gravel. Half-buried in it lies a huge cylinder about thirty yards across, crusted in dun-coloured, ashy scale and surrounded by the splintered remains of a fir tree. Scattered pines stand around, and the low sun is just clearing them towards Weybridge. Far off to the east a strip of heather smoulders, sending up a thin blue thread of smoke. There is no wind and no birdsong.
why: The text describes this exterior as wonderfully still and empty, a strange and luminous early-morning contrast to the dark observatory.
excerpts: The early morning was wonderfully still, and the sun, just clearing the pine trees towards Weybridge, was already warm.
The Thing itself lay almost entirely buried in sand, amidst the scattered splinters of a fir tree it had shivered to fragments in its descent.
An enormous hole had been made by the impact of the projectile, and the sand and gravel had been flung violently in every direction over the heath
The heather was on fire eastward, and a thin blue smoke rose against the dawn.

title: The dining room at Maybury
place: A comfortable late-Victorian suburban dining room in the narrator's house on Maybury Hill. A table is laid with a white cloth, silver and glassware, and a cold dinner sits untouched. A lamp with a pink shade casts a warm rosy glow over the table. A glass of crimson-purple wine stands by one place, beside a dish of nuts. Beyond the lamplight the room fades into soft shadow, and the summer night is dark outside.
why: It is a warm, lamplit, domestic interior that the narrator remembers with photographic vividness as his last civilised dinner, unlike the night observatory and the sunlit heath.
excerpts: peering at me from under the pink lamp shade, the white cloth with its silver and glass table furniture
for in those days even philosophical writers had many little luxuries—the crimson-purple wine in my glass, are photographically distinct.
The dinner, which was a cold one, had already been served, and remained neglected on the table
At the end of it I sat, tempering nuts with a cigarette
